city.name: Shinjuku
city.description: Shinjuku from open data, lit by the real sun: Nishi-Shinjuku's towers at Project PLATEAU's surveyed heights, Kabukicho's arch, the east exit's screens, 2-chome, Shinjuku Gyoen, Jingu Gaien and, in Yotsuya, the Suga Shrine stairs of Your Name.

tour.title: Shinjuku, from open data
tour.text: {buildings} buildings. {share:plateau}% of the footprint area stands at a height that Project PLATEAU surveyed, on GSI's laser-scanned bare earth under GSI aerial photographs.

tour.title: The stairs of Suga Shrine
tour.text: {landmark:suga.otokozaka.steps} stone steps, three and a half metres wide, red iron handrails both sides and down the middle: the 男坂 of Suga Shrine, the stairs of Your Name. The film turns ten this year.

tour.title: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
tour.text: Kenzo Tange's city hall, finished in 1991: one tower that splits in two at the 33rd floor, 243 m high, with a free observation deck in each half at 202 m. It was the tallest building in Tokyo until 2007.

tour.title: Kabukicho after dark
tour.text: Kabukicho Ichibangai's red arch has lit the way in since 1969. The district is named for a kabuki theatre planned after the war that was never built.

protection.title: No sun-access rule for public places
protection.summary: Tokyo protects no park's sunlight. The windows are a lunch-hour thought experiment for this project, as in the Marunouchi model.
protection.source_note: Windows are our own choice (noon to 13:00, all year), not law. The Building Standards Act's shadow rule (日影規制, art. 56-2) limits hours of shadow on neighbouring land in residential-type zones; it does not cover public places and does not apply in commercial districts such as Shinjuku.
protection.reading_note: Tokyo keeps standard time all year.
protection.tip: Tip: try a tower beside Shinjuku Gyoen's west gate.

shore.encoding: r: 128 + 2 x signed distance to the shoreline (m, water positive); g: sand; b: rock

trees.note: Species are not mapped; the mix is a guess from the cities' street-tree surveys and the parks' own guides: ginkgo and zelkova (keyaki) are Japan's commonest street trees, with plane trees and camphor; the woods are the laurel forest's evergreen broadleaves and camphors, with zelkovas, black pines, maples and a few cedars (sugi, standing for hinoki too). Areas give the parks and precincts known for their own trees a mix of their own; their outlines are OpenStreetMap's (pipeline/tree_areas.py).

areas.name: Shinjuku Gyoen
areas.note: The French formal garden's plane avenues, the Japanese garden's pines, the Himalayan cedars (sugi stands in) and camphors.

areas.name: Meiji Jingu Gaien
areas.note: The ginkgo avenue to the Seitoku Memorial Picture Gallery, gold in late November.

areas.name: Meiji Jingu
areas.note: The planted shrine forest, now mostly camphor and the evergreen oaks and shii of the laurel forest.
